comparison: Strong agreement on in vitro slice culture findings (C2, C25-C38). Both evaluations find the evidence for β-CTF-induced spine loss requiring BACE1 co-expression to be well-supported. OpenEval notes converging evidence from multiple approaches; peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'conclusions of the in vitro experiments using cultured hippocampal slices were well supported by the data.'

Agreement on Aβ-independence in vitro (C3, C39-C54). Both evaluations accept the evidence that β-CTF causes spine loss independently of Aβ in slice cultures. OpenEval emphasizes γ-secretase inhibitor experiments and APP mutants; peer reviewers confirm findings 'support the contribution of beta-CTF-dependent but non-Abeta dependent process.'

Major disagreement on in vivo findings (C4, C55-C60). OpenEval finds the in vivo data and electrophysiology supported with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge these claims, stating 'Evidence that the detrimental effects in mice are directly caused by β-CTF rather than indirectly via Aβ is critical' and noting the absence of γ-secretase inhibitor experiments in vivo makes results 'incomplete and hence less convincing.'

Disagreement on behavioral findings and Aβ exclusion (C5, C61-C76, C103). OpenEval finds behavioral data supported with adequate controls and accepts absence of plaques as evidence against Aβ involvement. Peer reviewers question this: 'The absence of plaque formation (Fig. 4C) is not sufficient to exclude the possibility that Aβ is involved' and note studies are 'inconclusive because potential effects of Aβ generated by γ-secretase cleavage of β-CTF were not considered.'

Agreement on endosomal mechanism (C78-C86). Both evaluations accept the evidence for endosomal dysfunction via the YENPTY motif. OpenEval finds β-CTFmut experiments 'particularly compelling'; peer reviewers confirm authors 'confirmed previous research' on this mechanism, though Reviewer 2 notes the analysis is 'interesting but primitive.'

Partial overlap on protein changes and Rab5 rescue. OpenEval R6 addresses protein level changes (C87-C92) and notes uncertainty about causality. Peer R6 addresses both protein changes and Rab5 rescue (C87-C99), accepting the data but noting limited depth. Both find evidence supported but with reservations about mechanistic completeness.

Agreement on Rab5 rescue experiment (C93-C99, C117-C118). OpenEval emphasizes the rescue as 'critical test of the proposed mechanism' demonstrating causal role of endosomal dysfunction. Peer reviewers do not explicitly critique the Rab5S34N rescue data, implying acceptance, though they note overall mechanistic analysis is 'primitive.'

Agreement on behavioral test results (C69-C75). OpenEval R4 includes behavioral findings as part of comprehensive in vivo assessment with adequate sample sizes. Peer R7 notes these behavioral findings are not questioned by reviewers and appear to be implicitly accepted as secondary observations.

Disagreement on clinical implications (C104-C108). OpenEval rates these claims as UNCERTAIN, noting they are 'logical inferences but not directly tested.' Peer reviewers are more critical, with Reviewer 1 challenging clinical relevance by noting BACE1 inhibitors worsened cognition, 'suggesting that β-CTF could facilitate learning and memory,' and the editor noting 'application of the findings is limited.'

Agreement on BACE1 inhibitor trial context (C109-C112). Both evaluations accept these claims describing clinical trial outcomes and complexity of BACE1 inhibition. OpenEval notes explanations are 'speculative but supported by citations'; peer reviewers reference this context and suggest considering studies on physiological roles of BACE1, indicating agreement with the complexity.

OpenEval R8 addresses background claims about AD pathology (C6-C10) as well-established knowledge with authoritative citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not evaluate background/contextual claims.

OpenEval R9 addresses recent clinical trial results (C11-C15, C100-C102) as accurately summarized with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these contextual claims about external clinical data are not specifically evaluated by peer reviewers.

OpenEval R10 addresses established APP processing pathways (C16-C19, C27-C29) as supported by citations and Human Protein Atlas data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers do not typically evaluate well-established background biochemistry.

OpenEval R11 addresses prior literature on β-CTF and endosomal dysfunction (C20-C24, C77, C113-C116) as accurately summarized. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer R5 acknowledges C77 context. These are background claims providing study context.

OpenEval R12 addresses validation of experimental system showing predominant α-CTF from APP alone (C33). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; this technical validation claim is not specifically discussed by peer reviewers.

OpenEval R15 addresses therapeutic speculation (C119-C121) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are hypotheses requiring validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer reviewers focus on clinical relevance concerns in R8 but do not specifically evaluate these forward-looking therapeutic proposals.
